role.en: Patriarch; father of Israel and, in tradition, of many nations

summary.en: The first Hebrew patriarch. Called by God to leave Ur (or Haran) for Canaan under a covenant promise of land and descendants (Genesis 12). Scholars date the patriarchal setting loosely to the Middle Bronze Age (c. 2000-1800 BC) while debating the narratives' historicity and date of composition.

display.en: c. 2000–1800 BC (Middle Bronze Age; dating debated)

role.en: Matriarch; wife of Abraham, mother of Isaac

summary.en: Wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac, buried in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron (Genesis 23).

role.en: Patriarch; son of Abraham, father of Jacob and Esau

summary.en: The promised son of Abraham and Sarah, through whom the covenant line continued; father of Jacob and Esau.

role.en: Patriarch; father of the twelve tribes

summary.en: Son of Isaac, renamed 'Israel' after wrestling at the Jabbok (Genesis 32). His twelve sons are the eponymous ancestors of the tribes of Israel; famine drove his family to Egypt.

role.en: Patriarch; vizier of Egypt

summary.en: Son of Jacob, sold into Egypt and rising to high office, according to Genesis; the narrative frames Israel's settlement in Goshen and sets up the later bondage and Exodus.

role.en: Prophet and lawgiver; leader of the Exodus

summary.en: Leader who, in the biblical account, brought Israel out of Egyptian bondage, mediated the covenant and Law at Sinai, and led the people through the wilderness to the edge of Canaan, dying on Mount Nebo. The Exodus's date and historicity are debated.

display.en: c. 1400–1200 BC — depends on the exodus date

datingNote.en: Moses' dates move with the exodus date — c. 1446 BC on the early reading of 1 Kings 6:1, c. 1260 BC on the late reading of Exodus 1:11. The span shown covers both. The ascription of the Pentateuch to Moses is traditional; its composition history is debated.

role.en: Successor of Moses; led Israel into Canaan

summary.en: Moses' successor who, in the book bearing his name, led Israel across the Jordan near Jericho into Canaan.

display.en: c. 1400–1180 BC — depends on the exodus date

role.en: The first man; beginning of the genealogy that dates the Earth

summary.en: Formed by God on the sixth day (Genesis 1:26-27; 2:7). Genesis 5 gives his age at Seth's birth (130 years) and his whole life (930 years). Those intervals are the first step in the chronology that places Creation at 4004 BC and makes the Earth about six thousand years old.

datingNote.en: Years from the Genesis 5 genealogy on the Masoretic numbers (Ussher). The Septuagint's longer figures place Adam's creation roughly a millennium earlier. Archaeology does not assign Adam a year; the date is Scripture's.

role.en: Patriarch of the Flood; builder of the ark

summary.en: The righteous man of Genesis 6-9, warned of the coming Flood and commanded to build an ark of gopher wood, 300 cubits long (Genesis 6:14-15). He preserved his family and the animals through the deluge, landed on the mountains of Ararat, and received the rainbow covenant. The nations of Genesis 10 descend from his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth. Genesis 5 and 7 date him: 600 years old at the Flood, 950 years in all — 2948–1998 BC on Ussher's Masoretic sum.

datingNote.en: Years from the Genesis 5 and 11 genealogies on the Masoretic numbers (Ussher). Noah is 600 at the Flood (Genesis 7:6) and lives 950 years (Genesis 9:29). The Septuagint's longer figures shift the whole span earlier by about a thousand years. The excavated flood silt at Shuruppak (c. 2900 BC) is the material setting, not a rival birth year.

role.en: One of the Seven; the church's first martyr

summary.en: Chosen among the Seven to serve the Jerusalem church, 'full of faith and of the Holy Spirit'. Acts records that he 'did great wonders and signs among the people' (Acts 6:8) before his defence to the Sanhedrin and stoning — witnessed by the young Saul of Tarsus.

role.en: One of the Seven; evangelist of Samaria and the coast

summary.en: One of the Seven (distinct from Philip the apostle). Scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death, he proclaimed Christ in Samaria with exorcisms and healings (Acts 8:6-7), baptized the Ethiopian eunuch on the Gaza road, and settled at Caesarea, where Paul later lodged with him (Acts 21:8).

role.en: Disciple in Damascus who restored Saul's sight

summary.en: A devout disciple living in Damascus, sent in a vision to the blinded Saul of Tarsus on Straight Street. Laying hands on him, he restored Saul's sight and baptized him (Acts 9:10-19) — the hinge between the persecutor and the apostle.

role.en: Last of the judges; prophet who anointed Saul and David

summary.en: Raised at the sanctuary of Shiloh under Eli, Samuel judged Israel on a yearly circuit between Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah and his home at Ramah, anointed Saul as Israel's first king, and later anointed David at Bethlehem.

role.en: Court prophet to David and Solomon

summary.en: Delivered the dynastic promise to David, confronted him over Bathsheba and Uriah with the parable of the ewe lamb, and secured Solomon's succession against Adonijah.

realm.en: Kingdom of Israel under David and Solomon

role.en: Prophet who announced the division of the kingdom

summary.en: Tore his new garment into twelve pieces before Jeroboam to signify that ten tribes would be torn from Solomon's house, and later pronounced judgment on the dynasty he had helped raise.

role.en: Prophet of the Northern Kingdom under Ahab and Ahaziah

summary.en: Confronted Ahab and Jezebel over the worship of Baal through a three-year drought, the contest on Mount Carmel and the judgment on Naboth's vineyard; fled to Horeb, called Elisha at Abel-meholah, and was taken up beyond the Jordan.

role.en: Successor of Elijah; prophet through six reigns of Israel

summary.en: Called from the plough at Abel-meholah, he received a double portion of Elijah's spirit and worked for half a century across the Northern Kingdom — at Jericho, Shunem, Dothan and Samaria — advising kings, healing Naaman the Syrian, and setting Jehu's revolution in motion.

role.en: Prophet who alone foretold Ahab's death at Ramoth-gilead

summary.en: Summoned reluctantly before Ahab and Jehoshaphat, he contradicted four hundred court prophets and was imprisoned for it; Ahab died in the battle exactly as he had said.

role.en: Prophetess consulted over the book found in the temple

summary.en: When the book of the law was discovered during Josiah's temple repairs, the king's officials took it to Huldah in Jerusalem; her authentication of it set the reform in motion.

role.en: Judge and prophetess; the only woman to lead Israel in the judges period

summary.en: Judged Israel from beneath a palm between Ramah and Bethel, summoned Barak to face Sisera's chariots at the Kishon below Mount Tabor, and sang the victory song that is among the oldest poetry in the Hebrew Bible.

display.en: c. 1200–1125 BC — judges chronology is approximate

datingNote.en: The judges' terms are given as round numbers and may overlap regionally rather than run consecutively, so any absolute date for Deborah is a placement within the period, not a fix.

role.en: Judge who broke the Midianite raids

summary.en: Threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiders, he was called to tear down his father's altar of Baal and then routed the Midianite camp below the hill of Moreh with three hundred men, torches and trumpets.

display.en: c. 1191–1144 BC — judges chronology is approximate

datingNote.en: Dated only by the internal sequence of Judges, which gives round figures and may run in parallel across regions.

role.en: Judge of the Danite border against the Philistines

summary.en: A Nazirite from birth whose career was a running personal feud along the Philistine frontier, ending at Gaza when he pulled down the temple of Dagon.

display.en: c. 1120–1100 BC — judges chronology is approximate

datingNote.en: Placed late in the judges period by the Philistine setting; the absolute date is not recoverable.

role.en: Prophet of the wilderness; forerunner of Jesus

summary.en: Preached repentance and baptized in the Jordan, identified Jesus at his baptism, and was imprisoned and executed by Herod Antipas — an execution Josephus independently records.

role.en: Major prophet of Jerusalem, through four reigns of Judah

summary.en: Called in the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah advised Ahaz and Hezekiah through the Syro-Ephraimite war and Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC, insisting that Judah's security lay in trust rather than in alliances with Egypt or Assyria.

datingNote.en: Chapters 40–66 address the exile and the return, and most critical scholars assign them to later hands in the same tradition; others read the whole book as the 8th-century prophet's. The ministry dates here cover the figure of chapters 1–39, whose setting is fixed by the reigns named in Isaiah 1:1.

role.en: Major prophet of Judah's last forty years

summary.en: A priest's son from Anathoth, called in Josiah's thirteenth year, who watched the reform fail, the city besieged twice, and the temple burned. Imprisoned, thrown into a cistern, and finally carried into Egypt by the fleeing remnant against his own counsel.

datingNote.en: Lamentations is ascribed to Jeremiah by tradition (and by the Septuagint's superscription); the book itself is anonymous.

role.en: Major prophet of the exile, by the river Chebar

summary.en: A priest deported in 597 BC with Jehoiachin, who prophesied to the exile community in Babylonia — first that Jerusalem would certainly fall, then, once it had, of a valley of dry bones raised and a restored temple.

role.en: Exile in the Babylonian and Persian courts; visionary

summary.en: Taken to Babylon among the young men of the royal seed at the first deportation, he served under Nebuchadnezzar and into the Persian period, and the book bearing his name pairs court narratives with apocalyptic visions of successive empires.

datingNote.en: The book's own setting is the 6th century. Critical scholarship generally dates its composition, or at least chapters 7–12, to the Maccabean crisis of the 160s BC on the basis of its detailed Hellenistic references; conservative scholarship holds to a 6th-century composition. The dates here are those of the narrative setting.

role.en: Minor prophet to the Northern Kingdom in its last generation

summary.en: Prophesied through the collapse of Israel after Jeroboam II, making his own broken marriage the figure of a covenant Israel had abandoned — and of a love that would not let go.

role.en: Minor prophet of the day of the LORD

summary.en: Reads a locust plague as a summons to repentance and a foreshadowing of the day of the LORD, with the promise of the Spirit poured out on all flesh that Peter quotes at Pentecost.

display.en: date disputed: 9th century BC or post-exilic (c. 500–400 BC)

datingNote.en: Joel names no king, which is why its date is the most open in the Twelve. A 9th-century setting under Joash and a post-exilic setting after the temple's rebuilding are both well argued; the span shown covers both rather than choosing.

role.en: Herdsman of Judah sent to prophesy against Israel

summary.en: A sheep-breeder and dresser of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah, sent north to the royal sanctuary at Bethel to indict Israel's prosperity for resting on the ruin of the poor — and told by its priest to go home.

role.en: Minor prophet; the shortest book in the Hebrew Bible

summary.en: Twenty-one verses against Edom for standing by — and joining in — on the day Jerusalem fell.

realm.en: Edom and the survivors of Judah

display.en: c. 586–553 BC (an earlier 9th-century setting is also argued)

datingNote.en: The natural reading ties the oracle to Edom's conduct at Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC; a minority reads it against the earlier raid of 2 Chronicles 21 and dates it to the 9th century.

role.en: Minor prophet sent to Nineveh

summary.en: The one prophet of the Twelve whose book is a narrative about the prophet rather than a collection of his oracles: sent to Assyria's capital, he fled by sea for Tarshish, was brought back, preached, and then resented the mercy that followed. 2 Kings 14:25 places him under Jeroboam II.

display.en: c. 785–760 BC (the setting given by 2 Kings 14:25)

datingNote.en: The prophet is dated by 2 Kings 14:25 to Jeroboam II's reign. The book about him is widely dated later, on linguistic grounds, and read by many as a didactic narrative; that is a question about the book, not about where its events are set.

role.en: Minor prophet of the Judean lowlands

summary.en: A countryman from the Shephelah whose oracles run from the ruin of Samaria and the villages of the lowlands to the promise of a ruler from Bethlehem — and to the summary the tradition remembers best: to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly.

role.en: Minor prophet of Nineveh's fall

summary.en: An oracle against Assyria, whose capital fell to a Median-Babylonian coalition in 612 BC — read in Judah as the end of a century of tribute and terror.

display.en: c. 663–612 BC (between Thebes' fall and Nineveh's)

datingNote.en: Bracketed by the book itself: it looks back on the sack of Thebes (663 BC) and forward to Nineveh's fall (612 BC). Elkosh, the prophet's town, is unlocated.

role.en: Minor prophet who argued with God about justice

summary.en: Asks why God tolerates violence in Judah, is told the Chaldeans are coming, and asks how that can possibly be an answer — the book is the argument, ending in a psalm of trust without resolution.

display.en: c. 640–598 BC (Babylon rising, Jerusalem not yet fallen)

role.en: Minor prophet of Josiah's reign

summary.en: Announces a day of the LORD against Judah's syncretism and the surrounding nations, in the years of Josiah's reform.

role.en: Minor prophet of the temple's rebuilding

summary.en: In the second year of Darius he told a discouraged community that the half-built temple was the reason their own affairs went nowhere; the work resumed within a month.

display.en: 520 BC (dated to the month by the book itself)

role.en: Minor prophet alongside Haggai

summary.en: Began two months after Haggai with a series of night visions, urging the same rebuilding and looking beyond it to a cleansed city and a coming king riding on a donkey.

role.en: Last of the Twelve

summary.en: A disputation with a settled, disillusioned community about half-hearted offerings, broken marriages and withheld tithes, closing the Hebrew prophets with the promise of Elijah's return.

datingNote.en: 'Malachi' means 'my messenger' and may be a title rather than a name; the date rests on the book's setting — a functioning temple, a Persian governor, and the abuses Nehemiah also confronts.

role.en: First king of Israel

summary.en: Anointed by Samuel and acclaimed at Gilgal, he broke the Ammonite and Philistine pressure on the hill country but lost Samuel's backing, pursued David for years, and died with his sons on Mount Gilboa.

role.en: King of Judah and then of all Israel

summary.en: Anointed at Bethlehem while Saul still reigned, he rose through Saul's court, spent years as a fugitive in the Judean wilderness and a Philistine vassal at Ziklag, was made king at Hebron, took the Jebusite stronghold of Zion for his capital, and brought the ark there. The Tel Dan stele's reference to the 'house of David' is the earliest extra-biblical mention of the dynasty.

datingNote.en: Seventy-three psalms carry a Davidic superscription; the superscriptions are ancient but are not themselves part of the psalms, and how much of the Psalter goes back to David is debated.

role.en: King of Israel; builder of the first temple

summary.en: Succeeded David after Adonijah's failed bid, built the temple and palace complex in Jerusalem, and presided over the empire's high-water mark — at a cost in forced labour that split the kingdom the moment he died.

datingNote.en: Ascription of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song to Solomon is traditional; each book's own composition history is debated.

role.en: First king of Judah after the division

summary.en: His refusal at Shechem to lighten his father's levies split the kingdom; he kept Judah and Benjamin and lost the other ten tribes in a day.

role.en: First king of the Northern Kingdom

summary.en: Solomon's overseer of the forced levy, exiled to Egypt and recalled at the division, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so the northern tribes would not go up to Jerusalem — the sin every later king of Israel is measured against.

role.en: King of Israel; Elijah's antagonist

summary.en: Built Samaria into a regional power and married Jezebel of Sidon, whose Baal cult Elijah spent his ministry opposing. Assyrian records place him at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC with two thousand chariots — the earliest firm synchronism for an Israelite king.

role.en: Queen of Israel; daughter of Ethbaal of Sidon

summary.en: Brought the Tyrian Baal cult into the Israelite court, had the prophets of the LORD killed and Naboth judicially murdered for his vineyard, and died at Jezreel in Jehu's coup.

role.en: King of Israel; ended the house of Omri

summary.en: Anointed at Ramoth-gilead by Elisha's messenger, he killed Joram, Ahaziah and Jezebel and destroyed the Baal temple at Samaria. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III shows him — or his envoy — paying tribute in 841 BC, the only likely contemporary image of an Israelite king.

role.en: King of Israel at its greatest extent

summary.en: Restored Israel's borders 'from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain' in a long, prosperous reign — the reign Amos and Hosea address, and the one Jonah is dated to.

role.en: King of Judah through Sennacherib's invasion

summary.en: Centralized worship in Jerusalem, cut the Siloam tunnel to secure the city's water, and survived the Assyrian siege of 701 BC. Sennacherib's own prism boasts of shutting him up 'like a bird in a cage' — and does not claim to have taken the city.

role.en: Reforming king of Judah

summary.en: Came to the throne as a child, purged the high places, and centralized the Passover on Jerusalem after the book of the law was found during temple repairs. He was killed at Megiddo intercepting Pharaoh Necho in 609 BC.

role.en: Last king of Judah

summary.en: Installed by Nebuchadnezzar and pushed by his court into revolt, he watched the siege of 588–586 BC end in the burning of the temple; captured near Jericho, he was taken to Riblah, saw his sons killed, was blinded, and was carried to Babylon.

role.en: King of Babylon; took Jerusalem

summary.en: Broke Egyptian power at Carchemish in 605 BC and took Jerusalem three times — 605, 597 and 586 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle records the capture of 'the city of Judah' in his seventh year to the day, which is why this stretch of the chronology is the firmest in the Old Testament.

role.en: King who ended the exile

summary.en: Took Babylon in 539 BC and authorized subject peoples to return and rebuild their sanctuaries — the policy Ezra 1 records for Judah, and the Cyrus Cylinder states in general terms for Babylonia.

role.en: Governor who led the first return and rebuilt the temple

summary.en: Grandson of the exiled king Jehoiachin, he led the first company home under Cyrus' decree, laid the temple's foundation, and — prodded by Haggai and Zechariah — saw it finished in 516 BC.

role.en: Priest and scribe who brought the law back to Jerusalem

summary.en: Came up from Babylon with a royal commission, a caravan and the law, and read it aloud to the assembled people at the Water Gate — the beginning of a community defined by a text rather than a monarchy.

datingNote.en: Whether Ezra preceded or followed Nehemiah depends on which Artaxerxes his 'seventh year' belongs to; the traditional order (Ezra 458, Nehemiah 445) is followed here, with the reversal noted.

role.en: Cupbearer to Artaxerxes; rebuilt Jerusalem's walls

summary.en: Heard in the citadel at Susa that Jerusalem's walls were still broken, obtained a commission as governor, and rebuilt them in fifty-two days against sustained local opposition.

role.en: Jewish queen of Persia

summary.en: A Jewish exile who became queen to Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) and used that position to expose Haman's plot against her people — the origin of the feast of Purim.

realm.en: The Jewish community of the Persian empire

display.en: c. 483–473 BC (the reign of Xerxes I)

role.en: Benjaminite of Susa; Esther's guardian

summary.en: Sat in the king's gate, refused to bow to Haman, uncovered a plot against the king, and rose to be second in the empire.

realm.en: The Jewish community of the Persian empire

role.en: Jeremiah's scribe

summary.en: Wrote Jeremiah's oracles on a scroll and read them in the temple; when the king cut it up and burned it piece by piece, he wrote it out again with more added. A bulla bearing a 'Berechiah son of Neriah the scribe' is known, though its provenance is unprovenanced and disputed.

role.en: Apostle; brother of Simon Peter

summary.en: A fisherman of Bethsaida and a disciple of John the Baptist first, he brought his brother Simon to Jesus. Later tradition sends him to Scythia and the Black Sea coast and has him crucified at Patras.

realm.en: Galilee, then (by tradition) Scythia and Achaia

role.en: Apostle; first of the Twelve to be killed

summary.en: One of the three admitted to the transfiguration and Gethsemane; Herod Agrippa I had him killed with the sword around AD 44, the only apostle whose death the New Testament records.

role.en: Apostle; the disciple 'whom Jesus loved' in the Fourth Gospel

summary.en: Brother of James, one of the inner three, and by long tradition the evangelist of the Fourth Gospel, the three letters, and the Revelation given on Patmos. Tradition places his last years at Ephesus.

realm.en: Galilee, Jerusalem, then (by tradition) Asia Minor

datingNote.en: Authorship of the Johannine books is debated: the Gospel is anonymous, and Revelation names a 'John' on Patmos without identifying him as the apostle. The ascriptions here are the traditional ones, recorded as such.

role.en: One of the Twelve; from Bethsaida

summary.en: Called early and the one who brought Nathanael; tradition sends him to Phrygia and places his death at Hierapolis, where a first-century tomb and a martyrium have been excavated. Not to be confused with Philip the Evangelist, one of the Seven.

role.en: One of the Twelve

summary.en: Listed among the Twelve in all three synoptic lists and in Acts; generally identified with the Nathanael of the Fourth Gospel, called from under the fig tree. Traditions send him to Armenia and India.

role.en: One of the Twelve; 'doubting Thomas'

summary.en: Willing to go and die with Jesus at Bethany, absent at the first resurrection appearance and unwilling to believe on report — then the first in the Fourth Gospel to call Jesus God. A strong and early tradition sends him to India, where the Saint Thomas Christians trace their founding to him.

role.en: Apostle; tax collector at Capernaum

summary.en: Called from the tax booth on the Capernaum road — a customs post on the frontier between Antipas' Galilee and Philip's territory — and by tradition the author of the first Gospel.

datingNote.en: The first Gospel is formally anonymous; the ascription to Matthew is second-century and universal in the manuscripts, but it is a tradition rather than a claim the book makes.

role.en: One of the Twelve

summary.en: Named in every list of the Twelve and nowhere else in the New Testament; sometimes identified with 'James the less' of Mark 15:40, though the identification is not certain.

role.en: One of the Twelve

summary.en: Called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark and 'Judas not Iscariot' in Luke and John, where he asks at the last supper why Jesus will show himself to the disciples and not to the world.

role.en: One of the Twelve

summary.en: Distinguished from Simon Peter by an epithet that marks him either as a member of the zealot movement or simply as zealous for the law — with a tax collector among the same twelve.

role.en: One of the Twelve; betrayed Jesus

summary.en: Kept the common purse and handed Jesus over in Gethsemane for thirty pieces of silver. Matthew and Acts give differing accounts of his death and of the field bought with the money.

datingNote.en: Matthew 27:5 and Acts 1:18 differ on how Judas died and who bought the field; the app reports both rather than harmonizing them.

role.en: Chosen to replace Judas among the Twelve

summary.en: Selected by lot from among those who had accompanied Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension, so that the Twelve were complete before Pentecost.

role.en: Mother of Jesus

summary.en: Betrothed to Joseph when she conceived, present from Bethlehem to Cana to the cross, and among those gathered in the upper room after the ascension.

role.en: Carpenter of Nazareth; husband of Mary

summary.en: A τέκτων — a builder in wood and stone — who took Mary as his wife, brought the family to Egypt and back, and disappears from the narrative after the Passover visit when Jesus was twelve.

role.en: Disciple; first witness of the resurrection

summary.en: From Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, healed of seven demons, one of the women who supported the ministry out of their own means, present at the crucifixion, and the first to whom the risen Jesus appeared.

role.en: Leader of the Jerusalem church

summary.en: Not a follower during the ministry, but named in the earliest resurrection tradition and, by the council of Acts 15, the presiding voice in Jerusalem. Josephus records his execution by the high priest Ananus in AD 62.

role.en: Roman centurion of the Italian band at Caesarea

summary.en: A God-fearing officer whose household received the Spirit before baptism — the episode that settled, for Peter and then for Jerusalem, that Gentiles were to be admitted without becoming Jews first.

role.en: Dealer in purple at Philippi; first named convert in Europe

summary.en: A trader in the expensive purple cloth of her home city, met at the riverside place of prayer outside Philippi; her household was baptized and her house became the first church in Macedonia.

role.en: Tentmakers; co-workers of Paul

summary.en: A married couple expelled from Rome under Claudius' edict, who worked at the same trade as Paul in Corinth, travelled with him to Ephesus, taught Apollos 'the way of God more perfectly', and hosted churches in their house in three cities.

role.en: Alexandrian Jew; eloquent teacher at Ephesus and Corinth

summary.en: Knowing only John's baptism, he was instructed by Priscilla and Aquila and became a powerful advocate in Achaia — and, without wanting it, the name of one of the factions Paul rebukes at Corinth.
